machines.title: Binary increment
machines.description: Adds one to a binary number written with the least significant bit first, so that the carry moves in the same direction as the head. It is the first example in the lecture of the course and the first machine of the 2024 simulator; Fig. 1.1 steps through it.

machines.title: Multiples of three
machines.description: An enumerator for the multiples of three in unary, from task 2a of the first exercise sheet. Each time the machine enters its output state, the tape holds the next word of the list, starting with the empty word.

machines.title: aⁿbⁿ
machines.description: An enumerator for the language of the words aⁿbⁿ, from task 2b of the first exercise sheet. It lists the words in order of increasing n, obtaining each from the previous one by adding one a in front and one b at the end.

machines.title: Unary multiplication
machines.description: The machine A_mul from task 3 of the first exercise sheet, which multiplies two numbers in unary by repeated addition. This exercise is the origin of the project; Fig. 1.2 runs the machine with decimal input and output.

machines.title: Doubling on one tape
machines.description: The machine M*2 on a single tape, computing xⁿ ↦ x²ⁿ (task 4b of the first exercise sheet). It moves one x at a time and walks across the growing output for every input symbol, so its number of steps grows quadratically in n.

machines.title: Doubling on two tapes
machines.description: The machine M*2 with two tapes (task 4a of the first exercise sheet). It copies the input to the second tape while reading it and then writes one x for each copied x, so its number of steps grows linearly in n; Fig. 1.3 compares both versions.

machines.title: Parity in unary
machines.description: The machine A_mod2 from task E of the third exercise sheet, computing xⁿ ↦ x^(n mod 2) in unary. It erases the input from the right, keeps the parity of the number of erased symbols in its state, and writes a single x at the end if that number is odd.

machines.title: Palindromes
machines.provenance: Classic exercise, written for this project
machines.description: An acceptor for the palindromes over a and b. It compares the first and the last remaining symbol, erases both and repeats, so its number of steps grows quadratically with the length of the input.

machines.title: aⁿbⁿcⁿ
machines.provenance: Classic exercise, written for this project
machines.description: An acceptor for the words aⁿbⁿcⁿ, a language that is not context-free. In each round it marks one a, one b and one c, and it accepts when all symbols are marked at the same time.

machines.title: Binary addition
machines.provenance: Classic exercise, written for this project
machines.description: A transducer that adds two binary numbers, written with the most significant bit first and separated by +. It adds the bits of the second number to the first one at a time, from the right, and lets carries run to the left.

machines.title: Binary increment, most significant bit first
machines.provenance: Classic exercise, written for this project
machines.description: Adds one to a binary number written with the most significant bit first. The head runs to the right end of the input and then carries to the left; the playground opens with this machine.

machines.title: BB(1) champion
machines.description: The busy beaver champion for one state: it writes a 1, moves and halts after 1 step, leaving 1 one.

machines.title: BB(2) champion
machines.description: The two-state champion, which attains both S(2) = 6 and Σ(2) = 4. Lecture 2 of the course uses it, without its halting transition, to show Σ(2) = 4.

machines.title: BB(3) champion
machines.provenance: bbchallenge wiki, BB(3), the champion for the number of steps S(3)
machines.description: A three-state machine that attains S(3) = 21. It leaves 5 ones, fewer than Σ(3) = 6: no three-state machine attains both maxima.

machines.title: Σ(3) champion
machines.provenance: bbchallenge wiki, BB(3), a champion for the number of ones Σ(3)
machines.description: A three-state machine that leaves Σ(3) = 6 ones. It halts after 14 steps, earlier than the machines that attain S(3) = 21.

machines.title: BB(4) champion
machines.description: The four-state champion, which attains both S(4) = 107 and Σ(4) = 13, as Brady proved.

machines.title: BB(5) champion
machines.description: The five-state champion found by Marxen and Buntrock. It halts after 47,176,870 steps with 4,098 ones, and the bbchallenge collaboration proved in Coq that no five-state machine runs longer.

machines.title: BB(2,3) champion
machines.description: The champion for two states and three symbols. It halts after 38 steps, the largest number possible for this class.

machines.title: BB(2,4) champion
machines.description: The champion for two states and four symbols. It halts after 3,932,964 steps, the largest number possible for this class.

machines.title: BB(6) champion
machines.provenance: bbchallenge wiki, BB(6), the champion found by mxdys in June 2025
machines.description: The current champion for six states, found by mxdys in June 2025. It is known to halt, and its running time establishes S(6) > 10↑↑10↑↑10↑↑8, far more than can be simulated step by step, so the gallery shows the beginning of its run.

machines.title: Antihydra
machines.description: A six-state cryptid whose halting problem is a Collatz-like question about the map h ↦ ⌊3h/2⌋ started at 8. Whether it halts is open; chapter 6 explains the rule.

machines.title: Hydra
machines.description: A cryptid with two states and five symbols that follows the same map as Antihydra from a different starting value, with the roles of even and odd values exchanged. Whether it halts is open.

machines.title: Bigfoot
machines.description: A cryptid with three states and three symbols whose behaviour follows a Collatz-like rule. Whether it halts is open.

machines.title: Wolfram's (2,3) machine
machines.provenance: Wolfram's 2-state 3-symbol machine, rule 596440, as published for the Wolfram 2,3 Turing Machine Research Prize
machines.description: Wolfram's machine with two states and three symbols, which has no halting transition. Smith proved it universal in an extended sense that requires an infinite, non-periodic initial tape; whether this counts as universality has been debated, as chapter 2 explains.
